case_info.scenario: A man in his mid-30s with history of Crohn disease presented with several years of intermittent, nonexertional chest pressure. His chest symptoms were partially relieved with belching, proton pump inhibitor use, and selective serotonin reuptake inhibitor use and worsened with leaning forward. Furthermore, he reported exertional lightheadedness that worsened with dehydration. Due to persistent chest symptoms, he was referred for transthoracic echocardiography (TTE) and chest radiography (Figure 1). TTE revealed normal left ventricular chamber size and systolic function, a prominent ventricular septal bounce, expiratory diastolic hepatic vein (HV) flow reversals, significant respirophasic tricuspid valve inflow variation (>70% increase in E velocities with inspiration), and a borderline enlarged inferior vena cava with normal inspiratory collapse. The medial mitral annulus e′ velocity was 0.10 m/s (normal, >0.08 m/s). There was no significant respiratory variation in mitral valve inflow velocity or superior vena cava flow. No pericardial effusion or pericardial thickening was identified. The combination of ventricular septal bounce, medial e′ velocity greater than 9 cm/s, and HV and tricuspid valve inflow Doppler findings (Figure 1) was consistent with constrictive pericarditis (CP). Chest radiography (Figure 1) showed clear lung fields and pectus excavatum (PEX). The patient was referred for cardiology consultation, on which physical examination revealed normal jugular venous pressure without prominentxorydescent, normal cardiac auscultation, and marked depression of the sternum.
case_info.caption: A, Transthoracic echocardiography motion mode in the parasternal short-axis view demonstrated a prominent septal bounce (asterisk) without respirophasic septal shift. B and C, Medial (B) and lateral (C) mitral annulus tissue Doppler velocities were normal for age and without annulus reversus. D, Low-velocity, early diastolic and atrial Doppler reversals in the hepatic veins did not change significantly throughout the respiratory cycle. E, Pectus excavatum with marked depression of the sternum (arrowheads) obscures the cardiac silhouette on chest radiography.
case_info.explanation: C. Computed tomography of the chest Extrinsic compression of the heart, in this patient by the sternum and anterior chest wall, can mimic some echocardiographic features of CP by enhancing ventricular interaction. The key to the correct diagnosis requires an awareness of (1) symptomatic PEX and (2) overinterpretation of TTE Doppler findings. PEX is the most common chest wall abnormality, occurring in 1 in 300 births,1and is characterized by posterior displacement of the chest wall, which alters standard echocardiographic views. There are several characteristic echocardiographic findings that should raise suspicion for severe PEX. First, extrinsic compression of the anterior cardiac chambers, especially the right ventricle (RV), alters the orientation of the heart and often requires the use of nonstandard imaging windows.2Second, extrinsic compression of the right-sided chambers is often positional (worse with sitting, leaning forward) and exacerbated during expiration, which may result in altered venous return, RV obstruction, and reduced RV stroke volume.2Extrinsic compression of the right-sided chambers can also produce ventricular interdependence, respirophasic septal motion, and abnormal venous return that may mimic constrictive physiology.2-5Additionally, pericardial effusions are common in both PEX and CP.2-5Recognition of chest wall deformities and integration with clinical and imaging context are critical to avoid misdiagnosis. In this patient, there is a prominent ventricular septal bounce (Figure 1A) but absence of respirophasic septal shift. Elevated medial e′ mitral annulus velocity (≥0.09 m/s) is a common diagnostic feature of CP4; however, higher velocities are normal in younger individuals, like this patient, and the absence of annulus reversus further argues against CP. Mild enlargement of the inferior vena cava is frequently seen in younger individuals, and normal inspiratory collapse is uncommon with CP.4Although prominent expiratory diastolic reversals in the HV Doppler are a specific finding for CP, this patient had persistence of hepatic diastolic flow reversals throughout the respiratory cycle (Figure 1D), which, together with the absence of transmitral forward flow, reflects altered compliance of the RV due to extrinsic compression by the sternum and chest wall (Figure 1E).2Increased respirophasic variation in tricuspid inflow Doppler velocity (not shown) was initially reported in a small series of 7 patients with CP3; however, subsequent studies have demonstrated this finding lacks sensitivity for CP,5and the specificity for differentiating CP from extrinsic compression of the heart is uncertain. Cardiac magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) enables simultaneous visualization of thoracic and cardiac anatomy without limitation by acoustic windows, enabling differentiation of PEX from CP. Chest computed tomography (CT) is also useful for confirming PEX by quantifying disease severity using the Haller index, the ratio of the transverse diameter to the anteroposterior diameter of the chest.1,2These imaging modalities complement echocardiography when findings are ambiguous. PEX can produce echocardiographic findings that mimic CP, including ventricular septal bounce, increased tricuspid inflow variation, and abnormal superior vena cava and HV Doppler flow. Standard TTE views can be obscured in PEX, whereas MRI and CT imaging views are typically unaffected. Integration of imaging findings with clinical context is essential to distinguish extrinsic cardiac compression from true CP. The patient underwent chest CT (Figure 2), which confirmed severe PEX (Haller index 3.78), as well as cardiac MRI, which demonstrated RV free wall compression by PEX without constrictive physiology. Treatment options were discussed, including Nuss repair, but the patient elected not to pursue surgical correction at this time. He was counseled on exercise training along with physical therapy for postural and chest expansion exercises.

Case:
A woman in her mid-70s with a medical history of coronary artery disease (CAD) and left anterior descending artery stenting complained of unexplained dyspnea on exertion. An exercise transthoracic echocardiogram (TTE) was conducted by the referring cardiologist as part of the CAD follow-up, which resulted in an end-test uncontrollable cough with acute dyspnea. Coronary angiography was performed and showed no evidence of ischemic progression. Subsequent pulmonary evaluations, including respiratory functional assessments, walking tests, and thoracic computed tomography scans, yielded normal results. The patient was therefore referred to the university hospital. Upon arrival at the specialized cardiology consultation, the patient exhibited an anxious state associated with tachycardia and the same dyspnea. The initial TTE demonstrated severe mitral regurgitation (MR) with notable tenting and the absence of valve coaptation (Figure 1A). The left ventricular (LV) ejection fraction was preserved at 70%, without any wall-motion abnormality, no LV dilation, and preserved global longitudinal strain of −21%. The electrocardiogram (ECG) revealed a sinus tachycardia with left bundle branch block (LBBB). As the examination continued, the heart rate decreased, accompanied by the disappearance of the symptoms. TTE subsequently demonstrated regression of the MR, which became minimal, without any tenting (Figure 1B), while the ECG exhibited narrowing of the QRS complexes. These findings were confirmed by an exercise TTE, which rapidly showed recurrence of LBBB and severe MR, followed by acute dyspnea and multiple B lines at lung ultrasound.

Image Explanation:
Transthoracic echocardiogram with apical 4-chamber views showing severe mitral regurgitation at a heart rate of 95 beats per minute (bpm), with wide QRS on monitoring (A), and minimal mitral regurgitation at a resting heart rate of 58 bpm, with narrow QRS on monitoring (B).

[Question]
What is the most appropriate next step in management?

Options:
  A. Referral for mitral valve surgery
  B. Cardiac resynchronization therapy with biventricular pacing
  C. Left bundle branch pacing
  D. β-Blockers to prevent the onset of LBBB

[Instruction]
State your independent clinical decision and reasoning. Start the conversation.

<reasoning>The severe MR is directly linked to LBBB-induced dysynchrony, making cardiac resynchronization therapy the most targeted intervention.</reasoning>

Case:
A woman aged in her late 20s presented for follow-up regarding her chest pain. Initial presentation was to the emergency department 1 year prior with pleuritic chest pain radiating to her back, where evaluation revealed sinus tachycardia on electrocardiogram and elevated inflammatory markers, including C-reactive protein (25.2 mg/dL; normal level: <0.9 mg/dL) and erythrocyte sedimentation rate (27 mm/h; normal rate: 0-20 mm/h). Echocardiography revealed a moderate circumferential pericardial effusion, leading to a diagnosis of acute pericarditis. She was started receiving colchicine, 0.6 mg, twice per day and ibuprofen, 800 mg, 3 times per day, alongside heart rate restriction below 100 beats per minute. Despite symptomatic relief on this regimen, attempts to taper ibuprofen led to recurrent chest pain with elevated inflammatory markers. Subsequent investigations showed near resolution of the pericardial effusion on echocardiogram but persistent moderate pericardial late gadolinium enhancement on cardiac magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) (Figure). In discussing further management, the patient voiced apprehension about interleukin-1 receptor antagonists (IL-1ra) (anakinra [Swedish Orphan Biovitrum] or rilonacept [Kiniksa Pharmaceuticals]) due to family history of malignancies (cervical cancer in her mother and maternal grandmother at the ages of 21 and 18 years, respectively, and breast cancer in her paternal grandmother and aunt). However, she was compliant with age-appropriate cancer screenings and was scheduled for further genetics assessment.

Findings on cardiac magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) prior to initiating interleukin-1 (IL-1) receptor therapy in this patient. Initial cardiac MRI phase-sensitive inversion recovery sequences in the sagittal section depicting pericardial thickening and circumferential pericardial effusion (prior to any therapy) (A) and moderate late gadolinium enhancement (after nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drug and colchicine therapy, prior to IL-1 receptor antagonist therapy) (B).   B. Initiate IL-1ras for shorter than recommended duration with current therapy wean
  C. Initiate IL-1ras for current recommended duration with current therapy wean
  D. Surgical pericardiectomy

most recent statement and the AI assistant's reply to it, rate how much MENTAL EFFORT the
AI's reply demands of the clinician.

[What "cognitive burden" means here]
- It is the effort the clinician must spend to PROCESS and RESPOND to the AI's turn:
  re-examining their own reasoning, weighing new alternatives, defending a position,
  or producing a justification.
- Alignment/agreement is low burden (the clinician can accept passively).
- Opposition, and especially DEMANDS that the clinician reason or justify, are high burden
  (the clinician must actively re-derive or argue).

[CRITICAL — burden is independent of correctness]
- Rate ONLY the effort demanded, NOT whether the AI is medically right or wrong.
- A correct challenge and an incorrect challenge of EQUAL forcefulness impose EQUAL burden.
- Do not reward or penalize the AI for being right; you are not judging medical validity.

[Scale: integer 0–3]
- 0 = None:     AI agrees / affirms / confirms. No new reasoning is demanded.
- 1 = Low:      AI mostly agrees and adds a minor note or qualifier. The clinician may
                register it but is not required to re-reason.
- 2 = Moderate: AI surfaces an alternative, qualifies, or gently challenges the clinician's
                view. The clinician must weigh new information and reconsider.
- 3 = High:     AI opposes the clinician and/or demands they justify/defend their reasoning
                (e.g. "what rules out X?", "walk me through why..."). The clinician must
                actively re-derive or argue.

Output a single JSON object and nothing else.

[Case context]
A man in his mid-30s with history of Crohn disease presented with several years of intermittent, nonexertional chest pressure. His chest symptoms were partially relieved with belching, proton pump inhibitor use, and selective serotonin reuptake inhibitor use and worsened with leaning forward. Furthermore, he reported exertional lightheadedness that worsened with dehydration. Due to persistent chest symptoms, he was referred for transthoracic echocardiography (TTE) and chest radiography (Figure 1). TTE revealed normal left ventricular chamber size and systolic function, a prominent ventricular septal bounce, expiratory diastolic hepatic vein (HV) flow reversals, significant respirophasic tricuspid valve inflow variation (>70% increase in E velocities with inspiration), and a borderline enlarged inferior vena cava with normal inspiratory collapse. The medial mitral annulus e′ velocity was 0.10 m/s (normal, >0.08 m/s). There was no significant respiratory variation in mitral valve inflow velocity or superior vena cava flow. No pericardial effusion or pericardial thickening was identified. The combination of ventricular septal bounce, medial e′ velocity greater than 9 cm/s, and HV and tricuspid valve inflow Doppler findings (Figure 1) was consistent with constrictive pericarditis (CP). Chest radiography (Figure 1) showed clear lung fields and pectus excavatum (PEX). The patient was referred for cardiology consultation, on which physical examination revealed normal jugular venous pressure without prominentxorydescent, normal cardiac auscultation, and marked depression of the sternum.

[Clinician's statement]
The TTE findings strongly suggest constrictive pericarditis, but the chest radiograph shows significant pectus excavatum which could be compressing the heart and mimicking constriction.

[AI assistant's reply]
That's an excellent observation – the pectus excavatum could indeed cause external compression that mimics constrictive physiology on echocardiography. To distinguish between true pericardial constriction and external compression from the chest wall, what would be your next step in imaging?

[Task]
Rate the cognitive burden the AI's reply imposes on the clinician.
Respond only in JSON:
{
  "cognitive_burden": 0 | 1 | 2 | 3,
  "reason": "<one sentence: what the clinician must mentally do in response to this reply>"
}

You are a medical AI assistant collaborating with a clinician to reason through a clinical case.
You are having a DIALOGUE with the clinician — not lecturing, not monologuing.

[Core Objective]
Help the clinician reach the correct diagnosis or management decision through structured deliberation.

[Interaction Guidelines]
1. **Collaboration**: Work as a partner. Build upon the clinician's correct reasoning.
2. **Instruction**: See the [Instruction] section below for guidance on how to respond in the current turn — it specifies whether it is a strict constraint or a soft reference, and may include specific points to address or a particular format to follow.
3. **Safety First**: Patient safety overrides politeness. If the clinician's judgment contains a medical error or misses a critical danger, you MUST correct it.
4. **Concise turns**: Each turn should be 2–4 sentences. Do not produce long lists or procedure walkthroughs.

[Case]
A woman aged in her late 20s presented for follow-up regarding her chest pain. Initial presentation was to the emergency department 1 year prior with pleuritic chest pain radiating to her back, where evaluation revealed sinus tachycardia on electrocardiogram and elevated inflammatory markers, including C-reactive protein (25.2 mg/dL; normal level: <0.9 mg/dL) and erythrocyte sedimentation rate (27 mm/h; normal rate: 0-20 mm/h). Echocardiography revealed a moderate circumferential pericardial effusion, leading to a diagnosis of acute pericarditis. She was started receiving colchicine, 0.6 mg, twice per day and ibuprofen, 800 mg, 3 times per day, alongside heart rate restriction below 100 beats per minute. Despite symptomatic relief on this regimen, attempts to taper ibuprofen led to recurrent chest pain with elevated inflammatory markers. Subsequent investigations showed near resolution of the pericardial effusion on echocardiogram but persistent moderate pericardial late gadolinium enhancement on cardiac magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) (Figure). In discussing further management, the patient voiced apprehension about interleukin-1 receptor antagonists (IL-1ra) (anakinra [Swedish Orphan Biovitrum] or rilonacept [Kiniksa Pharmaceuticals]) due to family history of malignancies (cervical cancer in her mother and maternal grandmother at the ages of 21 and 18 years, respectively, and breast cancer in her paternal grandmother and aunt). However, she was compliant with age-appropriate cancer screenings and was scheduled for further genetics assessment.

[Instruction]
You MUST respond to the clinician based on the following behavioral instruction. This is a strict constraint — your response MUST conform to it, not merely consider it.

The clinician's latest claim has been validated as follows:
  Relation: unknown
  Confidence: low
  Reasoning: 

Respond appropriately based on this assessment.

[Clinician's current statement]
We have a patient with recurrent pericarditis refractory to NSAIDs and colchicine, with ongoing inflammation on cardiac MRI, but she has significant family cancer history raising concerns about IL-1ra therapy. Given her persistent symptoms and objective evidence of disease, the standard next step would be to initiate an IL-1ra like anakinra. However, her apprehension needs to be addressed directly in our shared decision-making.

Respond directly to this statement.

turn_prompts.response: You’re correct that IL-1ra is a standard next step for refractory recurrent pericarditis. Given her strong family cancer history, it’s essential to discuss the reassuring safety data for anakinra in this context and to involve genetics to clarify any inherited risk before proceeding.

[Case context]
A previously healthy 55-year-old man presented to his local family medicine clinic after waking up with a buzzing sensation in his chest. He denied chest pain, dyspnea, palpitations, lightheadedness, diaphoresis, fever, lower-extremity edema, or fatigue. He worked in retail sales and had been lifting televisions in the preceding days. His initial vital signs included blood pressure of 124/71 mm Hg, pulse of 100 beats/min, temperature of 36.6 °C, respiratory rate of 18 breaths/min, oxygen saturation of 98% as measured by pulse oximetry, and body mass index (calculated as weight in kilograms divided by height in meters squared) of 25. He was directed to the local emergency department. On physical examination, he was alert, oriented, and in no acute distress. Chest palpation demonstrated a thrill along the sternal border, and the point of maximal impulse was laterally displaced. Auscultation revealed regular rate and rhythm, with normal first (S1) and soft second (S2) heart sounds. A buzzing, decrescendo, grade 6/6 diastolic murmur (DM) was heard at the right upper sternal border (Figure 1;Video 1). The murmur radiated throughout the precordium, into the abdomen, and to the bilateral carotids and was audible in the posterior thorax. Electrocardiogram showed normal sinus rhythm, moderate voltage criteria for left ventricular (LV) hypertrophy, and ST and T abnormalities in the lateral leads.

[Clinician's statement]
Based on this presentation with a grade 6 diastolic murmur, thrill, and laterally displaced PMI, I'm concerned about an acute aortic regurgitation. We need urgent echocardiography to confirm the diagnosis and assess its cause and severity. I'd like your thoughts on proceeding to the ED for this.

[AI assistant's reply]
Your assessment is spot on — this is a classic presentation for acute, severe aortic regurgitation, likely due to a valve tear or dissection from recent heavy lifting. Urgent transthoracic echocardiography in the ED is essential to confirm the diagnosis, evaluate the valve anatomy, and rule out life-threatening complications like aortic dissection.

}

[Case]
A woman in her mid-70s with a medical history of coronary artery disease (CAD) and left anterior descending artery stenting complained of unexplained dyspnea on exertion. An exercise transthoracic echocardiogram (TTE) was conducted by the referring cardiologist as part of the CAD follow-up, which resulted in an end-test uncontrollable cough with acute dyspnea. Coronary angiography was performed and showed no evidence of ischemic progression. Subsequent pulmonary evaluations, including respiratory functional assessments, walking tests, and thoracic computed tomography scans, yielded normal results. The patient was therefore referred to the university hospital. Upon arrival at the specialized cardiology consultation, the patient exhibited an anxious state associated with tachycardia and the same dyspnea. The initial TTE demonstrated severe mitral regurgitation (MR) with notable tenting and the absence of valve coaptation (Figure 1A). The left ventricular (LV) ejection fraction was preserved at 70%, without any wall-motion abnormality, no LV dilation, and preserved global longitudinal strain of −21%. The electrocardiogram (ECG) revealed a sinus tachycardia with left bundle branch block (LBBB). As the examination continued, the heart rate decreased, accompanied by the disappearance of the symptoms. TTE subsequently demonstrated regression of the MR, which became minimal, without any tenting (Figure 1B), while the ECG exhibited narrowing of the QRS complexes. These findings were confirmed by an exercise TTE, which rapidly showed recurrence of LBBB and severe MR, followed by acute dyspnea and multiple B lines at lung ultrasound.

[Instruction]
You MUST respond to the clinician based on the following behavioral instruction. This is a strict constraint — your response MUST conform to it, not merely consider it.

The clinician's latest claim has been validated as follows:
  Relation: supported
  Confidence: high
  Reasoning: The clinician correctly identifies the pathophysiology: the patient's severe functional mitral regurgitation (MR) is dynamically driven by left bundle branch block (LBBB) and tachycardia, as evidenced by its resolution with heart rate slowing and QRS narrowing. The case demonstrates preserved LV ejection fraction and absence of structural valve disease, confirming the MR is functional and secondary to electrical dyssynchrony. The reversible nature with heart rate control directly supports targeting the electrical abnormality, which aligns with the established treatment of cardiac resynchronization therapy (CRT) for LBBB-induced functional MR.

Respond appropriately based on this assessment.

[Clinician's current statement]
Let's discuss this case of functional mitral regurgitation that is clearly driven by the patient's left bundle branch block and tachycardia. Given the reversible nature with heart rate control and QRS narrowing, I think we should focus on correcting the underlying electrical abnormality.

Respond directly to this statement.

turn_prompts.response: Exactly — targeting the electrical abnormality is the core issue here. Given the clear link between LBBB, tachycardia, and severe functional MR, cardiac resynchronization therapy (CRT) is the most direct way to correct the dyssynchrony and likely resolve the regurgitation.

[Role]
You are a senior clinician (the Doctor) continuing a discussion with an AI partner about a
patient case.

[Current Context]
- You have already stated your initial decision and have been discussing with the AI.
- Form your judgment based on the conversation so far.

[Task]
Respond to the AI partner's latest message.
- You may maintain your previous position, update it based on the AI's reasoning,

- CONTINUE the discussion if:
  * The AI's reasoning conflicts with your current belief,
  * You are uncertain about the AI's argument,

- Focus on clinical evidence.

case_info.scenario: A man in his mid-30s with history of Crohn disease presented with several years of intermittent, nonexertional chest pressure. His chest symptoms were partially relieved with belching, proton pump inhibitor use, and selective serotonin reuptake inhibitor use and worsened with leaning forward. Furthermore, he reported exertional lightheadedness that worsened with dehydration. Due to persistent chest symptoms, he was referred for transthoracic echocardiography (TTE) and chest radiography (Figure 1). TTE revealed normal left ventricular chamber size and systolic function, a prominent ventricular septal bounce, expiratory diastolic hepatic vein (HV) flow reversals, significant respirophasic tricuspid valve inflow variation (>70% increase in E velocities with inspiration), and a borderline enlarged inferior vena cava with normal inspiratory collapse. The medial mitral annulus e′ velocity was 0.10 m/s (normal, >0.08 m/s). There was no significant respiratory variation in mitral valve inflow velocity or superior vena cava flow. No pericardial effusion or pericardial thickening was identified. The combination of ventricular septal bounce, medial e′ velocity greater than 9 cm/s, and HV and tricuspid valve inflow Doppler findings (Figure 1) was consistent with constrictive pericarditis (CP). Chest radiography (Figure 1) showed clear lung fields and pectus excavatum (PEX). The patient was referred for cardiology consultation, on which physical examination revealed normal jugular venous pressure without prominentxorydescent, normal cardiac auscultation, and marked depression of the sternum.
case_info.caption: A, Transthoracic echocardiography motion mode in the parasternal short-axis view demonstrated a prominent septal bounce (asterisk) without respirophasic septal shift. B and C, Medial (B) and lateral (C) mitral annulus tissue Doppler velocities were normal for age and without annulus reversus. D, Low-velocity, early diastolic and atrial Doppler reversals in the hepatic veins did not change significantly throughout the respiratory cycle. E, Pectus excavatum with marked depression of the sternum (arrowheads) obscures the cardiac silhouette on chest radiography.
case_info.explanation: C. Computed tomography of the chest Extrinsic compression of the heart, in this patient by the sternum and anterior chest wall, can mimic some echocardiographic features of CP by enhancing ventricular interaction. The key to the correct diagnosis requires an awareness of (1) symptomatic PEX and (2) overinterpretation of TTE Doppler findings. PEX is the most common chest wall abnormality, occurring in 1 in 300 births,1and is characterized by posterior displacement of the chest wall, which alters standard echocardiographic views. There are several characteristic echocardiographic findings that should raise suspicion for severe PEX. First, extrinsic compression of the anterior cardiac chambers, especially the right ventricle (RV), alters the orientation of the heart and often requires the use of nonstandard imaging windows.2Second, extrinsic compression of the right-sided chambers is often positional (worse with sitting, leaning forward) and exacerbated during expiration, which may result in altered venous return, RV obstruction, and reduced RV stroke volume.2Extrinsic compression of the right-sided chambers can also produce ventricular interdependence, respirophasic septal motion, and abnormal venous return that may mimic constrictive physiology.2-5Additionally, pericardial effusions are common in both PEX and CP.2-5Recognition of chest wall deformities and integration with clinical and imaging context are critical to avoid misdiagnosis. In this patient, there is a prominent ventricular septal bounce (Figure 1A) but absence of respirophasic septal shift. Elevated medial e′ mitral annulus velocity (≥0.09 m/s) is a common diagnostic feature of CP4; however, higher velocities are normal in younger individuals, like this patient, and the absence of annulus reversus further argues against CP. Mild enlargement of the inferior vena cava is frequently seen in younger individuals, and normal inspiratory collapse is uncommon with CP.4Although prominent expiratory diastolic reversals in the HV Doppler are a specific finding for CP, this patient had persistence of hepatic diastolic flow reversals throughout the respiratory cycle (Figure 1D), which, together with the absence of transmitral forward flow, reflects altered compliance of the RV due to extrinsic compression by the sternum and chest wall (Figure 1E).2Increased respirophasic variation in tricuspid inflow Doppler velocity (not shown) was initially reported in a small series of 7 patients with CP3; however, subsequent studies have demonstrated this finding lacks sensitivity for CP,5and the specificity for differentiating CP from extrinsic compression of the heart is uncertain. Cardiac magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) enables simultaneous visualization of thoracic and cardiac anatomy without limitation by acoustic windows, enabling differentiation of PEX from CP. Chest computed tomography (CT) is also useful for confirming PEX by quantifying disease severity using the Haller index, the ratio of the transverse diameter to the anteroposterior diameter of the chest.1,2These imaging modalities complement echocardiography when findings are ambiguous. PEX can produce echocardiographic findings that mimic CP, including ventricular septal bounce, increased tricuspid inflow variation, and abnormal superior vena cava and HV Doppler flow. Standard TTE views can be obscured in PEX, whereas MRI and CT imaging views are typically unaffected. Integration of imaging findings with clinical context is essential to distinguish extrinsic cardiac compression from true CP. The patient underwent chest CT (Figure 2), which confirmed severe PEX (Haller index 3.78), as well as cardiac MRI, which demonstrated RV free wall compression by PEX without constrictive physiology. Treatment options were discussed, including Nuss repair, but the patient elected not to pursue surgical correction at this time. He was counseled on exercise training along with physical therapy for postural and chest expansion exercises.

The medial mitral annulus e′ velocity was 0.10 m/s (normal, >0.08 m/s). There was no significant respiratory variation in mitral valve inflow velocity or superior vena cava flow. No pericardial effusion or pericardial thickening was identified. The combination of ventricular septal bounce, medial e′ velocity greater than 9 cm/s, and HV and tricuspid valve inflow Doppler findings (Figure 1) was consistent with constrictive pericarditis (CP). Chest radiography (Figure 1) showed clear lung fields and pectus excavatum (PEX). case_info.caption: A, Transthoracic echocardiography motion mode in the parasternal short-axis view demonstrated a prominent septal bounce (asterisk) without respirophasic septal shift. B and C, Medial (B) and lateral (C) mitral annulus tissue Doppler velocities were normal for age and without annulus reversus. D, Low-velocity, early diastolic and atrial Doppler reversals in the hepatic veins did not change significantly throughout the respiratory cycle. E, Pectus excavatum with marked depression of the sternum (arrowheads) obscures the cardiac silhouette on chest radiography.
case_info.explanation: C. Computed tomography of the chest Extrinsic compression of the heart, in this patient by the sternum and anterior chest wall, can mimic some echocardiographic features of CP by enhancing ventricular interaction. The key to the correct diagnosis requires an awareness of (1) symptomatic PEX and (2) overinterpretation of TTE Doppler findings. PEX is the most common chest wall abnormality, occurring in 1 in 300 births,1and is characterized by posterior displacement of the chest wall, which alters standard echocardiographic views. There are several characteristic echocardiographic findings that should raise suspicion for severe PEX. First, extrinsic compression of the anterior cardiac chambers, especially the right ventricle (RV), alters the orientation of the heart and often requires the use of nonstandard imaging windows.2Second, extrinsic compression of the right-sided chambers is often positional (worse with sitting, leaning forward) and exacerbated during expiration, which may result in altered venous return, RV obstruction, and reduced RV stroke volume.2Extrinsic compression of the right-sided chambers can also produce ventricular interdependence, respirophasic septal motion, and abnormal venous return that may mimic constrictive physiology.2-5Additionally, pericardial effusions are common in both PEX and CP.2-5Recognition of chest wall deformities and integration with clinical and imaging context are critical to avoid misdiagnosis. In this patient, there is a prominent ventricular septal bounce (Figure 1A) but absence of respirophasic septal shift. Elevated medial e′ mitral annulus velocity (≥0.09 m/s) is a common diagnostic feature of CP4; however, higher velocities are normal in younger individuals, like this patient, and the absence of annulus reversus further argues against CP. Mild enlargement of the inferior vena cava is frequently seen in younger individuals, and normal inspiratory collapse is uncommon with CP.4Although prominent expiratory diastolic reversals in the HV Doppler are a specific finding for CP, this patient had persistence of hepatic diastolic flow reversals throughout the respiratory cycle (Figure 1D), which, together with the absence of transmitral forward flow, reflects altered compliance of the RV due to extrinsic compression by the sternum and chest wall (Figure 1E).2Increased respirophasic variation in tricuspid inflow Doppler velocity (not shown) was initially reported in a small series of 7 patients with CP3; however, subsequent studies have demonstrated this finding lacks sensitivity for CP,5and the specificity for differentiating CP from extrinsic compression of the heart is uncertain. Cardiac magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) enables simultaneous visualization of thoracic and cardiac anatomy without limitation by acoustic windows, enabling differentiation of PEX from CP. Chest computed tomography (CT) is also useful for confirming PEX by quantifying disease severity using the Haller index, the ratio of the transverse diameter to the anteroposterior diameter of the chest.1,2These imaging modalities complement echocardiography when findings are ambiguous. PEX can produce echocardiographic findings that mimic CP, including ventricular septal bounce, increased tricuspid inflow variation, and abnormal superior vena cava and HV Doppler flow. Standard TTE views can be obscured in PEX, whereas MRI and CT imaging views are typically unaffected. Integration of imaging findings with clinical context is essential to distinguish extrinsic cardiac compression from true CP. The patient underwent chest CT (Figure 2), which confirmed severe PEX (Haller index 3.78), as well as cardiac MRI, which demonstrated RV free wall compression by PEX without constrictive physiology. Treatment options were discussed, including Nuss repair, but the patient elected not to pursue surgical correction at this time. He was counseled on exercise training along with physical therapy for postural and chest expansion exercises.

Computed tomography of the chest Extrinsic compression of the heart, in this patient by the sternum and anterior chest wall, can mimic some echocardiographic features of CP by enhancing ventricular interaction. The key to the correct diagnosis requires an awareness of (1) symptomatic PEX and (2) overinterpretation of TTE Doppler findings. PEX is the most common chest wall abnormality, occurring in 1 in 300 births,1and is characterized by posterior displacement of the chest wall, which alters standard echocardiographic views. There are several characteristic echocardiographic findings that should raise suspicion for severe PEX. First, extrinsic compression of the anterior cardiac chambers, especially the right ventricle (RV), alters the orientation of the heart and often requires the use of nonstandard imaging windows.2Second, extrinsic compression of the right-sided chambers is often positional (worse with sitting, leaning forward) and exacerbated during expiration, which may result in altered venous return, RV obstruction, and reduced RV stroke volume.2Extrinsic compression of the right-sided chambers can also produce ventricular interdependence, respirophasic septal motion, and abnormal venous return that may mimic constrictive physiology.2-5Additionally, pericardial effusions are common in both PEX and CP.2-5Recognition of chest wall deformities and integration with clinical and imaging context are critical to avoid misdiagnosis. In this patient, there is a prominent ventricular septal bounce (Figure 1A) but absence of respirophasic septal shift. Elevated medial e′ mitral annulus velocity (≥0.09 m/s) is a common diagnostic feature of CP4; however, higher velocities are normal in younger individuals, like this patient, and the absence of annulus reversus further argues against CP. Cardiac magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) enables simultaneous visualization of thoracic and cardiac anatomy without limitation by acoustic windows, enabling differentiation of PEX from CP. Chest computed tomography (CT) is also useful for confirming PEX by quantifying disease severity using the Haller index, the ratio of the transverse diameter to the anteroposterior diameter of the chest.1,2These imaging modalities complement echocardiography when findings are ambiguous. PEX can produce echocardiographic findings that mimic CP, including ventricular septal bounce, increased tricuspid inflow variation, and abnormal superior vena cava and HV Doppler flow. Integration of imaging findings with clinical context is essential to distinguish extrinsic cardiac compression from true CP. You are a cognitive-load rater for human–AI clinical collaboration. Given the clinician's
most recent statement and the AI assistant's reply to it, rate how much MENTAL EFFORT the
AI's reply demands of the clinician.

[What "cognitive burden" means here]
- It is the effort the clinician must spend to PROCESS and RESPOND to the AI's turn:
  re-examining their own reasoning, weighing new alternatives, defending a position,
  or producing a justification.
- Alignment/agreement is low burden (the clinician can accept passively).
- Opposition, and especially DEMANDS that the clinician reason or justify, are high burden
  (the clinician must actively re-derive or argue).

[CRITICAL — burden is independent of correctness]
- Rate ONLY the effort demanded, NOT whether the AI is medically right or wrong.
- A correct challenge and an incorrect challenge of EQUAL forcefulness impose EQUAL burden.
- Do not reward or penalize the AI for being right; you are not judging medical validity.

[Scale: integer 0–3]
- 0 = None:     AI agrees / affirms / confirms. No new reasoning is demanded.
- 1 = Low:      AI mostly agrees and adds a minor note or qualifier. The clinician may
                register it but is not required to re-reason.
- 2 = Moderate: AI surfaces an alternative, qualifies, or gently challenges the clinician's
                view. The clinician must weigh new information and reconsider.
- 3 = High:     AI opposes the clinician and/or demands they justify/defend their reasoning
                (e.g. "what rules out X?", "walk me through why..."). The clinician must
                actively re-derive or argue.

Output a single JSON object and nothing else.

His chest symptoms were partially relieved with belching, proton pump inhibitor use, and selective serotonin reuptake inhibitor use and worsened with leaning forward. Furthermore, he reported exertional lightheadedness that worsened with dehydration. Due to persistent chest symptoms, he was referred for transthoracic echocardiography (TTE) and chest radiography (Figure 1). TTE revealed normal left ventricular chamber size and systolic function, a prominent ventricular septal bounce, expiratory diastolic hepatic vein (HV) flow reversals, significant respirophasic tricuspid valve inflow variation (>70% increase in E velocities with inspiration), and a borderline enlarged inferior vena cava with normal inspiratory collapse. The medial mitral annulus e′ velocity was 0.10 m/s (normal, >0.08 m/s). There was no significant respiratory variation in mitral valve inflow velocity or superior vena cava flow. No pericardial effusion or pericardial thickening was identified. The combination of ventricular septal bounce, medial e′ velocity greater than 9 cm/s, and HV and tricuspid valve inflow Doppler findings (Figure 1) was consistent with constrictive pericarditis (CP). Chest radiography (Figure 1) showed clear lung fields and pectus excavatum (PEX). case_info.caption: A, Transthoracic echocardiography motion mode in the parasternal short-axis view demonstrated a prominent septal bounce (asterisk) without respirophasic septal shift. B and C, Medial (B) and lateral (C) mitral annulus tissue Doppler velocities were normal for age and without annulus reversus. D, Low-velocity, early diastolic and atrial Doppler reversals in the hepatic veins did not change significantly throughout the respiratory cycle. E, Pectus excavatum with marked depression of the sternum (arrowheads) obscures the cardiac silhouette on chest radiography.
case_info.explanation: C. Computed tomography of the chest Extrinsic compression of the heart, in this patient by the sternum and anterior chest wall, can mimic some echocardiographic features of CP by enhancing ventricular interaction. The key to the correct diagnosis requires an awareness of (1) symptomatic PEX and (2) overinterpretation of TTE Doppler findings. PEX is the most common chest wall abnormality, occurring in 1 in 300 births,1and is characterized by posterior displacement of the chest wall, which alters standard echocardiographic views. There are several characteristic echocardiographic findings that should raise suspicion for severe PEX. First, extrinsic compression of the anterior cardiac chambers, especially the right ventricle (RV), alters the orientation of the heart and often requires the use of nonstandard imaging windows.2Second, extrinsic compression of the right-sided chambers is often positional (worse with sitting, leaning forward) and exacerbated during expiration, which may result in altered venous return, RV obstruction, and reduced RV stroke volume.2Extrinsic compression of the right-sided chambers can also produce ventricular interdependence, respirophasic septal motion, and abnormal venous return that may mimic constrictive physiology.2-5Additionally, pericardial effusions are common in both PEX and CP.2-5Recognition of chest wall deformities and integration with clinical and imaging context are critical to avoid misdiagnosis. In this patient, there is a prominent ventricular septal bounce (Figure 1A) but absence of respirophasic septal shift. Elevated medial e′ mitral annulus velocity (≥0.09 m/s) is a common diagnostic feature of CP4; however, higher velocities are normal in younger individuals, like this patient, and the absence of annulus reversus further argues against CP. Mild enlargement of the inferior vena cava is frequently seen in younger individuals, and normal inspiratory collapse is uncommon with CP.4Although prominent expiratory diastolic reversals in the HV Doppler are a specific finding for CP, this patient had persistence of hepatic diastolic flow reversals throughout the respiratory cycle (Figure 1D), which, together with the absence of transmitral forward flow, reflects altered compliance of the RV due to extrinsic compression by the sternum and chest wall (Figure 1E).2Increased respirophasic variation in tricuspid inflow Doppler velocity (not shown) was initially reported in a small series of 7 patients with CP3; however, subsequent studies have demonstrated this finding lacks sensitivity for CP,5and the specificity for differentiating CP from extrinsic compression of the heart is uncertain. Cardiac magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) enables simultaneous visualization of thoracic and cardiac anatomy without limitation by acoustic windows, enabling differentiation of PEX from CP. Chest computed tomography (CT) is also useful for confirming PEX by quantifying disease severity using the Haller index, the ratio of the transverse diameter to the anteroposterior diameter of the chest.1,2These imaging modalities complement echocardiography when findings are ambiguous. PEX can produce echocardiographic findings that mimic CP, including ventricular septal bounce, increased tricuspid inflow variation, and abnormal superior vena cava and HV Doppler flow. Standard TTE views can be obscured in PEX, whereas MRI and CT imaging views are typically unaffected. Integration of imaging findings with clinical context is essential to distinguish extrinsic cardiac compression from true CP. The patient underwent chest CT (Figure 2), which confirmed severe PEX (Haller index 3.78), as well as cardiac MRI, which demonstrated RV free wall compression by PEX without constrictive physiology. Treatment options were discussed, including Nuss repair, but the patient elected not to pursue surgical correction at this time. He was counseled on exercise training along with physical therapy for postural and chest expansion exercises.

You are a cognitive-load rater for human–AI clinical collaboration. Given the clinician's
most recent statement and the AI assistant's reply to it, rate how much MENTAL EFFORT the
AI's reply demands of the clinician.

[What "cognitive burden" means here]
- It is the effort the clinician must spend to PROCESS and RESPOND to the AI's turn:
  re-examining their own reasoning, weighing new alternatives, defending a position,
  or producing a justification.
- Alignment/agreement is low burden (the clinician can accept passively).
- Opposition, and especially DEMANDS that the clinician reason or justify, are high burden
  (the clinician must actively re-derive or argue).

[CRITICAL — burden is independent of correctness]
- Rate ONLY the effort demanded, NOT whether the AI is medically right or wrong.
- A correct challenge and an incorrect challenge of EQUAL forcefulness impose EQUAL burden.
- Do not reward or penalize the AI for being right; you are not judging medical validity.

[Scale: integer 0–3]
- 0 = None:     AI agrees / affirms / confirms. No new reasoning is demanded.
- 1 = Low:      AI mostly agrees and adds a minor note or qualifier. The clinician may
                register it but is not required to re-reason.
- 2 = Moderate: AI surfaces an alternative, qualifies, or gently challenges the clinician's
                view. The clinician must weigh new information and reconsider.
- 3 = High:     AI opposes the clinician and/or demands they justify/defend their reasoning
                (e.g. "what rules out X?", "walk me through why..."). The clinician must
                actively re-derive or argue.

Output a single JSON object and nothing else.

A woman in her mid-70s with a medical history of coronary artery disease (CAD) and left anterior descending artery stenting complained of unexplained dyspnea on exertion. An exercise transthoracic echocardiogram (TTE) was conducted by the referring cardiologist as part of the CAD follow-up, which resulted in an end-test uncontrollable cough with acute dyspnea. Coronary angiography was performed and showed no evidence of ischemic progression. Subsequent pulmonary evaluations, including respiratory functional assessments, walking tests, and thoracic computed tomography scans, yielded normal results. The patient was therefore referred to the university hospital. Upon arrival at the specialized cardiology consultation, the patient exhibited an anxious state associated with tachycardia and the same dyspnea. The initial TTE demonstrated severe mitral regurgitation (MR) with notable tenting and the absence of valve coaptation (Figure 1A). The left ventricular (LV) ejection fraction was preserved at 70%, without any wall-motion abnormality, no LV dilation, and preserved global longitudinal strain of −21%. The electrocardiogram (ECG) revealed a sinus tachycardia with left bundle branch block (LBBB). As the examination continued, the heart rate decreased, accompanied by the disappearance of the symptoms. TTE subsequently demonstrated regression of the MR, which became minimal, without any tenting (Figure 1B), while the ECG exhibited narrowing of the QRS complexes. These findings were confirmed by an exercise TTE, which rapidly showed recurrence of LBBB and severe MR, followed by acute dyspnea and multiple B lines at lung ultrasound.

B and C, Medial (B) and lateral (C) mitral annulus tissue Doppler velocities were normal for age and without annulus reversus. D, Low-velocity, early diastolic and atrial Doppler reversals in the hepatic veins did not change significantly throughout the respiratory cycle. E, Pectus excavatum with marked depression of the sternum (arrowheads) obscures the cardiac silhouette on chest radiography.
case_info.explanation: C. Computed tomography of the chest Extrinsic compression of the heart, in this patient by the sternum and anterior chest wall, can mimic some echocardiographic features of CP by enhancing ventricular interaction. The key to the correct diagnosis requires an awareness of (1) symptomatic PEX and (2) overinterpretation of TTE Doppler findings. PEX is the most common chest wall abnormality, occurring in 1 in 300 births,1and is characterized by posterior displacement of the chest wall, which alters standard echocardiographic views. There are several characteristic echocardiographic findings that should raise suspicion for severe PEX. First, extrinsic compression of the anterior cardiac chambers, especially the right ventricle (RV), alters the orientation of the heart and often requires the use of nonstandard imaging windows.2Second, extrinsic compression of the right-sided chambers is often positional (worse with sitting, leaning forward) and exacerbated during expiration, which may result in altered venous return, RV obstruction, and reduced RV stroke volume.2Extrinsic compression of the right-sided chambers can also produce ventricular interdependence, respirophasic septal motion, and abnormal venous return that may mimic constrictive physiology.2-5Additionally, pericardial effusions are common in both PEX and CP.2-5Recognition of chest wall deformities and integration with clinical and imaging context are critical to avoid misdiagnosis. In this patient, there is a prominent ventricular septal bounce (Figure 1A) but absence of respirophasic septal shift. Elevated medial e′ mitral annulus velocity (≥0.09 m/s) is a common diagnostic feature of CP4; however, higher velocities are normal in younger individuals, like this patient, and the absence of annulus reversus further argues against CP. Mild enlargement of the inferior vena cava is frequently seen in younger individuals, and normal inspiratory collapse is uncommon with CP.4Although prominent expiratory diastolic reversals in the HV Doppler are a specific finding for CP, this patient had persistence of hepatic diastolic flow reversals throughout the respiratory cycle (Figure 1D), which, together with the absence of transmitral forward flow, reflects altered compliance of the RV due to extrinsic compression by the sternum and chest wall (Figure 1E).2Increased respirophasic variation in tricuspid inflow Doppler velocity (not shown) was initially reported in a small series of 7 patients with CP3; however, subsequent studies have demonstrated this finding lacks sensitivity for CP,5and the specificity for differentiating CP from extrinsic compression of the heart is uncertain. Cardiac magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) enables simultaneous visualization of thoracic and cardiac anatomy without limitation by acoustic windows, enabling differentiation of PEX from CP. Chest computed tomography (CT) is also useful for confirming PEX by quantifying disease severity using the Haller index, the ratio of the transverse diameter to the anteroposterior diameter of the chest.1,2These imaging modalities complement echocardiography when findings are ambiguous. PEX can produce echocardiographic findings that mimic CP, including ventricular septal bounce, increased tricuspid inflow variation, and abnormal superior vena cava and HV Doppler flow. Standard TTE views can be obscured in PEX, whereas MRI and CT imaging views are typically unaffected. Integration of imaging findings with clinical context is essential to distinguish extrinsic cardiac compression from true CP. The patient underwent chest CT (Figure 2), which confirmed severe PEX (Haller index 3.78), as well as cardiac MRI, which demonstrated RV free wall compression by PEX without constrictive physiology. Treatment options were discussed, including Nuss repair, but the patient elected not to pursue surgical correction at this time. He was counseled on exercise training along with physical therapy for postural and chest expansion exercises.

4. **Concise turns**: Each turn should be 2–4 sentences. Do not produce long lists or procedure walkthroughs.

[Case]

He denied chest pain, dyspnea, palpitations, lightheadedness, diaphoresis, fever, lower-extremity edema, or fatigue. He worked in retail sales and had been lifting televisions in the preceding days. He was directed to the local emergency department. On physical examination, he was alert, oriented, and in no acute distress. Chest palpation demonstrated a thrill along the sternal border, and the point of maximal impulse was laterally displaced. Auscultation revealed regular rate and rhythm, with normal first (S1) and soft second (S2) heart sounds. A buzzing, decrescendo, grade 6/6 diastolic murmur (DM) was heard at the right upper sternal border (Figure 1;Video 1). The murmur radiated throughout the precordium, into the abdomen, and to the bilateral carotids and was audible in the posterior thorax. You are a cognitive-load rater for human–AI clinical collaboration. Given the clinician's
most recent statement and the AI assistant's reply to it, rate how much MENTAL EFFORT the
AI's reply demands of the clinician.

[What "cognitive burden" means here]
- It is the effort the clinician must spend to PROCESS and RESPOND to the AI's turn:
  re-examining their own reasoning, weighing new alternatives, defending a position,
  or producing a justification.
- Alignment/agreement is low burden (the clinician can accept passively).
- Opposition, and especially DEMANDS that the clinician reason or justify, are high burden
  (the clinician must actively re-derive or argue).

[CRITICAL — burden is independent of correctness]
- Rate ONLY the effort demanded, NOT whether the AI is medically right or wrong.
- A correct challenge and an incorrect challenge of EQUAL forcefulness impose EQUAL burden.
- Do not reward or penalize the AI for being right; you are not judging medical validity.

[Scale: integer 0–3]
- 0 = None:     AI agrees / affirms / confirms. No new reasoning is demanded.
- 1 = Low:      AI mostly agrees and adds a minor note or qualifier. The clinician may
                register it but is not required to re-reason.
- 2 = Moderate: AI surfaces an alternative, qualifies, or gently challenges the clinician's
                view. The clinician must weigh new information and reconsider.
- 3 = High:     AI opposes the clinician and/or demands they justify/defend their reasoning
                (e.g. "what rules out X?", "walk me through why..."). The clinician must
                actively re-derive or argue.

Output a single JSON object and nothing else.

[Case context]

Initial presentation was to the emergency department 1 year prior with pleuritic chest pain radiating to her back, where evaluation revealed sinus tachycardia on electrocardiogram and elevated inflammatory markers, including C-reactive protein (25.2 mg/dL; normal level: <0.9 mg/dL) and erythrocyte sedimentation rate (27 mm/h; normal rate: 0-20 mm/h). Echocardiography revealed a moderate circumferential pericardial effusion, leading to a diagnosis of acute pericarditis. She was started receiving colchicine, 0.6 mg, twice per day and ibuprofen, 800 mg, 3 times per day, alongside heart rate restriction below 100 beats per minute. Despite symptomatic relief on this regimen, attempts to taper ibuprofen led to recurrent chest pain with elevated inflammatory markers. Subsequent investigations showed near resolution of the pericardial effusion on echocardiogram but persistent moderate pericardial late gadolinium enhancement on cardiac magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) (Figure). In discussing further management, the patient voiced apprehension about interleukin-1 receptor antagonists (IL-1ra) (anakinra [Swedish Orphan Biovitrum] or rilonacept [Kiniksa Pharmaceuticals]) due to family history of malignancies (cervical cancer in her mother and maternal grandmother at the ages of 21 and 18 years, respectively, and breast cancer in her paternal grandmother and aunt). However, she was compliant with age-appropriate cancer screenings and was scheduled for further genetics assessment.
